title: Trump: One America News tells new employee to be pro-Russia
description_short: Trump: One America News tells new employee to be pro-Russia
description_medium: Former One America News Network writer Ernest Champell told The Daily Beast that on his first day a colleague greeted him with, “Yeah, we like Russia here.” Champell said he joined around 2016 and left after four months, objecting to OAN’s favorable coverage of Russian propaganda. His account describes one employee’s remark and his impression of the newsroom, not a written policy governing the network’s reporting.
description_long: In an interview published in 2019, former One America News Network writer Ernest Champell recalled a colleague greeting him on his first day with, “Yeah, we like Russia here.” Champell said he joined OAN around 2016 and left after about four months because he objected to what he saw as the network’s support for Russian propaganda. The Daily Beast based its account on interviews with former OAN employees, and the timeline places the remark during a period when the Seth Rich conspiracy was circulating. The anecdote gives a first-person account of an explicitly pro-Russia sentiment within one U.S. television newsroom. It does not establish that OAN had a formal instruction to take that position, that all staff shared it, or that the remark determined any particular story. Nor does the remark itself prove coordination with Russian officials. It is evidence of what Champell says he heard and how he understood the outlet’s culture; broader claims about OAN’s coverage or outside direction require other records.

title: Trump: New York Times editor changes FBI's Russia story to cover for Trump
description_short: Trump: New York Times editor changes FBI's Russia story to cover for Trump
description_medium: In September 2016, FBI officials met New York Times reporter Eric Lichtblau after learning that the paper was preparing a story on possible links between the Trump Organization and Alfa Bank. The bureau asked him to delay publication, saying the story might interfere with its investigation. The Times published a substantially revised article after editor Dean Baquet sought more evidence; motive to protect Trump is not established by the supplied account.
description_long: In September 2016, FBI officials arranged to meet New York Times reporter Eric Lichtblau after a source told the bureau that the paper was preparing a story about possible connections between the Trump Organization and Alfa Bank. The FBI was investigating ties between Russia and the Trump campaign and asked Lichtblau to delay publication because it feared interference with that inquiry. Lichtblau’s editor, Dean Baquet, wanted more evidence as the election approached; Lichtblau argued publication had become more important because it concerned an FBI investigation. According to the timeline’s account of Lichtblau’s later reporting, the story nearly stalled, then ran on October 31 after Harry Reid publicly criticized FBI Director James Comey. Lichtblau said the published story differed substantially from what he had filed and omitted the computer scientists’ account of possible communications between the Trump Organization and Alfa Bank. These details support that the FBI sought delay and the editor revised the story. The claim that Baquet changed it specifically to cover for Trump is the timeline’s interpretation; the material does not establish his motive.
notes: Reason: The account describes a delay request and a substantially revised article but does not establish that Baquet’s motive was to protect Trump.
Proposed correction: Attribute the claim about editorial motive and describe the documented sequence without presenting the alleged intent as fact.

title: Trump: Rep. Dana Rohrabacher meets with Julian Assange for a pardon quid pro quo
description_short: Trump: Rep. Dana Rohrabacher meets with Julian Assange for a pardon quid pro quo
description_medium: Rep. Dana Rohrabacher met Julian Assange, Charles Johnson and Assange’s lawyer at Ecuador’s London embassy in August 2017. Rohrabacher later said he hoped Assange could provide evidence about the 2016 WikiLeaks releases; Assange reportedly sought assurance he would not be arrested. A Senate inquiry found no evidence supporting Rohrabacher’s or Assange’s theories. Accounts differ on whether a presidential pardon was offered or only discussed.
description_long: On August 16, 2017, Rep. Dana Rohrabacher met Julian Assange and activist Charles Johnson at Ecuador’s embassy in London; Assange’s lawyer was also present. The meeting concerned Assange’s offer to provide material about the 2016 WikiLeaks releases and whether Russia was involved. Rohrabacher later said he hoped the meeting could help him test his theory about how the emails were obtained. The Senate Intelligence Committee reported that Assange wanted an assurance he would not be arrested if he left the embassy and that Rohrabacher promised to ask the White House about arranging one. Rohrabacher said he was not permitted to speak with President Trump and did not communicate further with Assange about a potential deal. The committee said it found no evidence supporting Rohrabacher’s theory or Assange’s claims. A later video was reported to show Rohrabacher offering a presidential pardon in exchange for a denial of Russian involvement, but the record leaves unclear who initiated that idea. The meeting is established; a completed quid pro quo is not.
notes: Reason: The meeting is documented, but whether a pardon-for-information quid pro quo was actually offered remains disputed in the supplied account.
Proposed correction: Describe the meeting and reported pardon discussion with attribution; do not present an agreed exchange as established.

title: Trump: Former staffer says Trump used Adderall and touched teen pageant contestants
description_short: Trump: Former staffer says Trump used Adderall and touched teen pageant contestants
description_medium: Former Apprentice production staffer Noel Casler has accused Donald Trump of using Adderall and behaving inappropriately toward teenage beauty-pageant contestants. Casler described his work around pageants and made the claims in public remarks. The allegations remain unverified in the supplied material, which names no contemporaneous records or independent witnesses. They should be presented as Casler’s accusations rather than established conduct.
description_long: Former Apprentice staffer Noel Casler made public allegations about Donald Trump’s conduct at beauty pageants and alleged misuse of Adderall. Casler said he had worked with Trump before and during the television show and had also worked at pageants in the 1990s. He described Trump examining contestants and making sexualized comments, and separately alleged that Trump crushed and snorted Adderall. These are serious claims about past conduct and drug use, attributed to Casler; the account does not independently verify them. It refers generally to people who knew Casler before his allegations but does not identify them or provide specific corroborating evidence. The timeline does not give dates for the alleged incidents, records supporting the drug claim, or a response from Trump. It does not name the contestants Casler described. The accusations should therefore be reported as Casler’s account, not as established facts about Trump’s conduct or health.
notes: Reason: The serious claims are attributed to Casler, but the supplied account gives no dates, named corroborating witnesses, supporting records or response from Trump.
Proposed correction: Keep the claims explicitly attributed to Casler and avoid stating them as established conduct or medical fact.

title: Trump: Ghislaine Maxwell appears in staged photo with CIA book
description_short: Trump: Ghislaine Maxwell appears in staged photo with CIA book
description_medium: The New York Post reported that Ghislaine Maxwell was photographed at an In-N-Out restaurant in Los Angeles shortly after Jeffrey Epstein died, reading a book about CIA operatives. The story prompted questions about the photo’s origin; later reporting cited inconsistencies and an expert’s view that it showed signs of editing. The image and the book do not establish that Maxwell or Epstein worked for an intelligence agency, and the material gives no link to Trump.
description_long: The New York Post reported in August 2019 that Ghislaine Maxwell had been photographed at an In-N-Out restaurant in Los Angeles two days after Jeffrey Epstein’s death, reading Ted Gup’s book about CIA operatives. The image drew attention because of the timing and the book’s subject. The TrumpFile account says later reviews by The Daily Mail and Inside Edition identified inconsistencies in the photograph and story, and that a forensic photo expert saw signs of editing. It raises the possibility that Maxwell’s friend and attorney Leah Saffian took or altered the image and sold it to the Post, but those explanations are possibilities rather than settled facts. Neither Maxwell’s appearance in the photo nor her choice of book establishes a relationship with the CIA or proves that Epstein worked for an intelligence service. The episode provides no documented connection to Trump. Without a verified account of how the image was made and published, the title’s claim that it was staged should remain qualified.
notes: Reason: The linked account reports inconsistencies and possible editing but does not settle the photo’s provenance or establish a connection to Trump.
Proposed correction: Attribute the sighting and editing claims, and remove the “Trump:” framing unless a supported connection is supplied.
